items.headline: CBP Expanding CAPE for Reconciliation Entries by June 29
items.summary: CBP informed the Court of International Trade on June 9 that it is expanding CAPE functionality to process IEEPA tariff refunds for entries flagged for reconciliation, with the capability expected to be available on June 29. Since CAPE Phase 1 launched, more than 16 million entries have been processed and approximately $22 billion in refunds have been completed. Over $89 billion in potential and certified IEEPA duty refunds have been accepted for processing.

items.headline: Trump Administration Appeals CIT's Universal IEEPA Refund Order
items.summary: On June 2, 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice formally appealed the CIT's order compelling CBP to refund $166 billion in IEEPA tariffs to the Federal Circuit, challenging both the universal refund order and CBP Commissioner testimony requirement. DOJ also filed a motion asking for an expedited ruling on the CBP Commissioner's testimony issue by Friday, June 5. This creates uncertainty for importers with finally liquidated entries who may now need individual court orders to obtain refunds.

items.headline: CBP Reverses Position on Finally Liquidated Entry Refunds
items.summary: On May 29, 2026, CBP filed a motion asserting for the first time that it lacks legal authority to issue IEEPA refunds on finally liquidated entries (180+ days past liquidation) without importer-specific court judgments. For importers counting on the refund process to eventually cover finally liquidated entries, CBP's new position is a significant setback requiring individual federal court cases. This contradicts CBP's published guidance indicating finally liquidated entries would be included in upcoming CAPE phases.

items.headline: Latest CAPE Progress: $85B Processed, 8.5M Entries Liquidated
items.summary: As of May 26, 2026, CBP reported that $85 billion in potential and certified IEEPA refunds have been accepted for CAPE processing, with $20.6 billion in refund claims completed and sent to Treasury for disbursement. Nearly 16 million entries passed CAPE validations, with approximately 8.5 million liquidated without IEEPA duties. Over 4,000 consolidated refunds haven't been transmitted to Treasury due to missing ACH banking information.

items.headline: CIT Orders CBP Commissioner to Testify June 9
items.summary: Judge Eaton issued a "show cause" order requiring CBP to explain why the court should not lift suspension of its universal refund order and directed CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott to appear in court on June 9. The order requires the Commissioner to answer questions regarding the agency's implementation of the tariff refund process. This hearing could determine whether CBP must immediately process refunds for all entries, including finally liquidated ones.

items.headline: Government Appeal Deadline Passes
items.summary: The government's deadline to appeal the CIT's nationwide IEEPA refund order ran through June 7, 2026, with any appeal expected to challenge the CIT's authority to mandate refunds nationwide. A successful appeal could result in a stay of the refund process and significantly delay payments. With the appeal now filed, importers face continued uncertainty about the scope and timing of refunds.

items.headline: First CAPE Refunds Hitting Bank Accounts
items.summary: CBP launched CAPE on April 20, 2026, with ACH refund payments beginning as early as May 12, 2026, though some media reports suggest certain importers may already be receiving refunds. Importers should anticipate that valid IEEPA refunds are generally issued within 60-90 days following CAPE Declaration acceptance, unless compliance concerns require further review. However, substantial refund exposure remains tied up in CAPE validation and future phases.

items.headline: Section 122 Replacement Tariffs Also Struck Down
items.summary: President Trump imposed a 10% import surcharge under Section 122 of the Trade Act beginning February 24, 2026, following IEEPA tariff invalidation. However, in a May 7, 2026 decision, the CIT held the Section 122 global tariffs were unlawful because statutory conditions for a "balance of payments deficit" were not satisfied. The CIT determined the administration relied on an overly broad interpretation of Section 122. This creates additional refund exposure for importers who paid replacement tariffs.
